front.title: IKEv2 negotiation for Bound End-to-End Tunnel (BEET) mode ESP

abstract.t: This document specifies a new Notify Message Status Type for the Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2), to negotiate IPsec ESP Bound End-to-End Tunnel (BEET) mode. BEET mode combines the benefits of tunnel mode with reduced overhead, making it suitable for applications requiring minimalistic end-to-end tunnels and multi-address multi-homing capabilities. The introduction of the USE_BEET_MODE Notify Message Status Type enables the negotiation and establishment of BEET mode security associations.

section.title: Introduction
section.t: The Bound End-to-End Tunnel (BEET) mode is specified in . BEET mode was first standardized in Appendix B of . It offers an optimized approach for deploying IP Security (IPsec) using Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) for end-to-end use cases. It combines the advantages of Tunnel and Transport modes specified in , while minimizing their overhead for end-to-end use cases.

This document specifies the necessary code points to negotiate an ESP BEET mode SA using the Internet Key Exchange Protocol Version 2 (IKEv2) , by introducing a new Notify Message Status Type, USE_BEET_MODE, to facilitate the negotiation and establishment of BEET mode security associations in IKEv2.

section.title: Background
section.t: BEET mode is already used for end-to-end security in HIP environments , where it is set up by the HIP key exchange rather than by IKE. It is also deployed with IKEv2 using a private Notify Message Status Type, as implemented in . This document defines the IKEv2 negotiation.
This private-use deployment has been in use for a long time. This document requests an IANA-assigned Notify Message Status Type value, [TBD1], for the USE_BEET_MODE notification.

Additionally, BEET mode ESP is valuable for low-power devices which usually use only one end-to-end IPsec tunnel, as it reduces power consumption and complexity. In situations where devices or IPsec connections are dedicated to a single application or transport protocol, the use of BEET mode simplifies packet processing and conserves energy, especially benefiting lower-powered devices.

section.t: The key words "MUST", "MUST NOT", "REQUIRED", "SHALL", "SHALL NOT", "SHOULD", "SHOULD NOT", "RECOMMENDED", "NOT RECOMMENDED", "MAY", and "OPTIONAL" in this document are to be interpreted as described in BCP 14 when, and only when, they appear in all capitals, as shown here.

section.title: IKEv2 Negotiation
section.t: When negotiating a Child SA using IKEv2, the new "USE_BEET_MODE" Notify Message Status Type is used to negotiate BEET mode for the Child SA pair. The method used is similar to how USE_TRANSPORT_MODE is negotiated, as described in .

To request a BEET-mode SA on the Child SA pair, the initiator MUST include the USE_BEET_MODE Notify Message Status Type when requesting a new Child SA, either during the IKE_AUTH or the CREATE_CHILD_SA exchanges to create a new Child SA. If the request is accepted, the response MUST also include a USE_BEET_MODE Notify Message Status Type. If the responder declines and does not include the USE_BEET_MODE notification in the response, the Child SA will be established in Tunnel mode. If Tunnel mode is unacceptable to the initiator, the initiator MUST delete the Child SA via a subsequent INFORMATIONAL exchange with a Delete payload, as specified in .

A responder for which Tunnel mode is not an acceptable fallback for this Child SA MAY, during a CREATE_CHILD_SA exchange, instead reject the request by returning a NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN notification, in which case no Child SA is created. During the IKE_AUTH exchange, the responder SHOULD instead follow the Tunnel-mode fallback described above, since rejecting the Child SA via NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN would leave the IKE SA established without any Child SA.

When rekeying a Child SA that was established with BEET mode, the TSi and TSr of the replacement Child SA MUST be identical to those of the Child SA being replaced, since the inner addresses bound to a BEET mode Security Association are fixed for its lifetime .

The USE_BEET_MODE notification MUST NOT be combined with other Child SA mode notifications, such as USE_TRANSPORT_MODE or USE_AGGFRAG , in the same request. As BEET mode is currently specified only in terms of Tunnel mode Security Association and Traffic Selector semantics , its interaction with these other modes is not defined.

If a responder nonetheless receives a request containing the USE_BEET_MODE notification together with one or more other Child SA mode notifications, it MUST select at most one of these notifications, or none of them -- in which case the Child SA is established in Tunnel mode -- and include only that single notification, if any, in its response.

If, contrary to the above, the response includes the USE_BEET_MODE notification together with any other Child SA mode notification, the response is ambiguous as to which mode the responder has selected; the initiator MUST treat the response as invalid and MUST delete the Child SA. In either case -- whether the responder omitted USE_BEET_MODE (resulting in Tunnel mode, as described above) or returned such an ambiguous response -- the initiator can determine acceptability immediately upon processing the response. It MAY therefore delete the Child SA without first installing it.

section.title: Traffic Selectors
section.t: A BEET mode Security Association binds the Child SA to a single, fixed pair of inner addresses for its lifetime . This is in contrast to Tunnel mode, where the Traffic Selectors negotiate address ranges and the inner addresses of any given packet may be any pair of addresses within those ranges. For this reason, the Traffic Selectors (TSi and TSr) of a Child SA negotiated with the USE_BEET_MODE notification MUST each specify, after narrowing if applicable, a single IP address -- that is, a Starting Address equal to the Ending Address (equivalent to a /32 or /128 prefix), as defined in Section 3.13.1 of -- which become the inner addresses bound to the Child SA.

The initiator MAY propose TSi and TSr that already each specify a single IP address, or MAY propose broader Traffic Selectors and rely on the responder to narrow them, as described in Section 2.9 of . If the responder selects USE_BEET_MODE, the TSi and TSr returned in its response MUST each specify a single IP address, regardless of how the corresponding Traffic Selectors were proposed in the request. If the proposed Traffic Selectors cannot be narrowed to a single address acceptable to the responder's policy, the responder MUST NOT include the USE_BEET_MODE notification in its response, resulting in Tunnel mode (or NO_PROPOSAL_CHOSEN, per the responder's policy as described above).

The initiator MUST verify that, when the response includes the USE_BEET_MODE notification, the TSi and TSr returned in the response each specify a single IP address. If they do not, the response is invalid; as with an ambiguous USE_BEET_MODE response described above, the initiator MUST delete the Child SA.

A MOBIKE address update for the IKE SA and its Child SAs changes only the outer addresses used to reach the peer. The TSi and TSr of a BEET mode Child SA, and the inner addresses they represent, are unaffected by such an update and MUST NOT be renegotiated as part of it.

section.title: USE_BEET_MODE Notify Message Payload
section.t: The USE_BEET_MODE Notify Message Status Type uses the Notify Payload format defined in Section 3.10 of . The Protocol ID and SPI Size fields MUST be set to 0 and MUST be ignored if not 0. The notification carries no Notification Data.

section.title: IANA Considerations
section.t: This document defines a new Notify Message Status Type, to be added to the "Notify Message Status Types" registry .

section.title: Security Considerations
section.t: This document defines only the IKEv2 negotiation of BEET mode. The security properties of BEET mode itself are discussed in . This section follows the guidelines of .
There are no known new vulnerabilities that the addition of the BEET mode to IKEv2 would create.

An initiator whose USE_BEET_MODE request repeatedly results in a response it must reject, as described in Section 2, SHOULD NOT retry the request indefinitely, to avoid Child SA creation and deletion churn with that peer.

Falling back to Tunnel mode when USE_BEET_MODE is not negotiated is functionally complete in most deployments, at the cost of the header-compression and address-mapping optimizations BEET mode provides. In some use cases, however -- such as Host Identity Protocol (HIP) deployments that rely on these address mappings -- the fallback may result in a loss of functionality beyond these optimizations. Whether such a loss is acceptable for a given deployment is outside the scope of IKEv2 negotiation.

front.title: Key words for use in RFCs to Indicate Requirement Levels

abstract.t: In many standards track documents several words are used to signify the requirements in the specification. These words are often capitalized. This document defines these words as they should be interpreted in IETF documents. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Ambiguity of Uppercase vs Lowercase in RFC 2119 Key Words

abstract.t: RFC 2119 specifies common key words that may be used in protocol specifications. This document aims to reduce the ambiguity by clarifying that only UPPERCASE usage of the key words have the defined special meanings.

This document describes version 2 of the Internet Key Exchange (IKE) protocol. IKE is a component of IPsec used for performing mutual authentication and establishing and maintaining Security Associations (SAs). This document obsoletes RFC 5996, and includes all of the errata for it. It advances IKEv2 to be an Internet Standard.

front.title: A Bound End-to-End Tunnel (BEET) mode for ESP

abstract.t: This document is an update to the Bound End-to-End Tunnel (BEET) mode for ESP in as described in [RFC7402]. It brings the description in alignment with the addition of BEET mode for IKEv2 without any processing changes as described in [RFC7402]

front.title: Guidelines for Writing RFC Text on Security Considerations

abstract.t: All RFCs are required to have a Security Considerations section. Historically, such sections have been relatively weak. This document provides guidelines to RFC authors on how to write a good Security Considerations section. This document specifies an Internet Best Current Practices for the Internet Community, and requests discussion and suggestions for improvements.

front.title: Using the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) Transport Format with the Host Identity Protocol (HIP)

abstract.t: This memo specifies an Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) based mechanism for transmission of user data packets, to be used with the Host Identity Protocol (HIP). This document obsoletes RFC 5202.

front.title: Improving Awareness of Running Code: The Implementation Status Section

abstract.t: This document describes a simple process that allows authors of Internet-Drafts to record the status of known implementations by including an Implementation Status section. This will allow reviewers and working groups to assign due consideration to documents that have the benefit of running code, which may serve as evidence of valuable experimentation and feedback that have made the implemented protocols more mature.

This process is not mandatory. Authors of Internet-Drafts are encouraged to consider using the process for their documents, and working groups are invited to think about applying the process to all of their protocol specifications. This document obsoletes RFC 6982, advancing it to a Best Current Practice.

This document specifies the details of the Host Identity Protocol (HIP). HIP allows consenting hosts to securely establish and maintain shared IP-layer state, allowing separation of the identifier and locator roles of IP addresses, thereby enabling continuity of communications across IP address changes. HIP is based on a Diffie-Hellman key exchange, using public key identifiers from a new Host Identity namespace for mutual peer authentication. The protocol is designed to be resistant to denial-of-service (DoS) and man-in-the-middle (MitM) attacks. When used together with another suitable security protocol, such as the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP), it provides integrity protection and optional encryption for upper-layer protocols, such as TCP and UDP.
This document obsoletes RFC 5201 and addresses the concerns raised by the IESG, particularly that of crypto agility. It also incorporates lessons learned from the implementations of RFC 5201.

This document describes the minimal properties that an IP Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) implementation needs to meet to remain interoperable with the standard ESP as defined in RFC 4303. Such a minimal version of ESP is not intended to become a replacement of ESP in RFC 4303. Instead, a minimal implementation is expected to be optimized for constrained environments while remaining interoperable with implementations of ESP. In addition, this document provides some considerations for implementing minimal ESP in a constrained environment, such as limiting the number of flash writes, handling frequent wakeup and sleep states, limiting wakeup time, and reducing the use of random generation.
This document does not update or modify RFC 4303. It provides a compact description of how to implement the minimal version of that protocol. RFC 4303 remains the authoritative description.

front.title: Aggregation and Fragmentation Mode for Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) and Its Use for IP Traffic Flow Security (IP-TFS)

abstract.t: This document describes a mechanism for aggregation and fragmentation of IP packets when they are being encapsulated in Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP). This new payload type can be used for various purposes, such as decreasing encapsulation overhead for small IP packets; however, the focus in this document is to enhance IP Traffic Flow Security (IP-TFS) by adding Traffic Flow Confidentiality (TFC) to encrypted IP-encapsulated traffic. TFC is provided by obscuring the size and frequency of IP traffic using a fixed-size, constant-send-rate IPsec tunnel. The solution allows for congestion control, as well as nonconstant send-rate usage.

This document describes the MOBIKE protocol, a mobility and multihoming extension to Internet Key Exchange (IKEv2). MOBIKE allows the IP addresses associated with IKEv2 and tunnel mode IPsec Security Associations to change. A mobile Virtual Private Network (VPN) client could use MOBIKE to keep the connection with the VPN gateway active while moving from one address to another. Similarly, a multihomed host could use MOBIKE to move the traffic to a different interface if, for instance, the one currently being used stops working. [STANDARDS-TRACK]

front.title: Security Architecture for the Internet Protocol

abstract.t: This document describes an updated version of the "Security Architecture for IP", which is designed to provide security services for traffic at the IP layer. This document obsoletes RFC 2401 (November 1998). [STANDARDS-TRACK]

This document describes an updated version of the Encapsulating Security Payload (ESP) protocol, which is designed to provide a mix of security services in IPv4 and IPv6. ESP is used to provide confidentiality, data origin authentication, connectionless integrity, an anti-replay service (a form of partial sequence integrity), and limited traffic flow confidentiality. This document obsoletes RFC 2406 (November 1998). [STANDARDS-TRACK]
